text: It was Grimalkin who gave the first warning, low and sharp from his usual watch-post, and within moments the whole camp had shifted into the particular practiced readiness that a year of genuine danger had taught them all to summon without needing to discuss it first.
“Rider,” Long John reported, low, watching from the treeline. “Alone. Older man, moving slow — either exhausted or being careful. Hard to tell which from here.”
“Could be nothing,” Marian said, already reaching for her bow regardless. “Could be considerably worse than nothing. We don't take chances on the difference.”

They met him at the camp's edge, weapons ready but not yet raised, the particular controlled tension of people who had learned, through hard experience, exactly how quickly an ordinary afternoon could turn into something else entirely.

The stranger reined in his horse at a respectful distance, hands visible, posture carrying none of the confidence of a man expecting trouble to favor him. He was older than Marian had first guessed from a distance — weathered in a way that spoke of considerably more than simple age, features carrying the particular hard-worn quality of a man who had spent years quietly carrying something heavy.

“I'm looking for my son,” he said, and something in his voice, tired and careful and entirely without threat, made even Marian's raised guard falter slightly. “Robin. Robin of Loxby. I'm told this is where I might find him.”
The name landed like a stone dropped into still water, and Robin, standing near the back of the gathered group, felt every part of him go suddenly, completely still.

sequence._describe: Robin of Loxby staring in shocked recognition at the weathered older man, complicated emotions crossing both their faces, the crew watching in tense silence. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, tense emotional daytime lighting, shocked poignant mood.

text: “Father,” Robin said, the word coming out strange and unfamiliar in his own mouth, as though he'd forgotten, somewhere along the way, exactly how it was meant to sound.

The man's face did something complicated at that — relief and grief and a dozen years of careful distance all working across his features at once. “Robin,” he said, quiet, and took an instinctive step forward before visibly catching himself, uncertain of his own welcome. “You've grown. I don't know why that surprises me. It's been long enough.”

“It has,” Robin said, and found, to his own considerable confusion, that he couldn't properly settle on a single feeling to anchor the moment — not the cold anger he might have expected of himself, not simple joy, but something tangled and uncertain that refused to resolve into anything clean.

“Why are you here?” Robin asked, finally, the question coming out harder than he'd quite intended, old hurt surfacing despite himself. “After all this time. After everything. You simply — appear, after years of silence, and expect what, precisely? A warm welcome?”

“No,” the man said, steady despite the visible weight the question cost him. “I expect nothing, Robin. I've no right to expect anything from you at all, and I know that better than anyone standing here could tell me. I'm here because you're in danger, and I'd rather be the one to warn you properly than let you learn it from men considerably less concerned with your welfare than I am.”
Marian, watching closely, saw something shift behind Robin's guarded expression — anger still present, but genuine alarm beginning to work its way in alongside it.

sequence._describe: Robin's father explaining the urgent danger to the crew, Will Scarlett-Sleeves stepping forward with protective suspicion, real tension in the gathered group. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, tense earnest daytime lighting, urgent serious mood.

text: “What danger?” Robin asked, and though his voice still carried real wariness, something in it had shifted toward the practical urgency the question actually required.

“The Sheriff knows,” the man said, plainly. “Who you are. Where you came from. He's had a Captain investigating you — thoroughly, by every account I've managed to gather — and she's uncovered rather more of our family's history than either of us would have liked reaching his attention. He knows you're my son, Robin. He's preparing to move on that knowledge, and I couldn't in good conscience let that reach you without warning first.”
“How do you know all this?” Will asked, stepping forward with careful protectiveness, watching the stranger with real, unconcealed suspicion.

“Because it's my debt he's collecting on,” the man said, quiet. “Whatever else you don't yet understand about why I'm standing here, understand that much plainly. This danger is mine before it was ever properly yours.”

“What debt?” Robin asked, and there was real, raw urgency in it now, years of unanswered questions finally finding an opening he hadn't expected to arrive so abruptly. “What history? You've spent my entire life refusing to properly explain anything, and now you arrive with warnings about danger and debts and expect me to simply accept it without understanding any of it?”
The man was quiet a long moment, something old and exhausted and finally, visibly, resolved settling across his weathered features.

“You deserve the whole truth,” he said, finally. “All of it. Not simply the urgent pieces I've managed to arrive with today. I came prepared to warn you of danger, Robin, but I find, standing here now, that I owe you considerably more than a warning. I owe you an explanation years overdue, and I don't intend to leave here again without finally giving it to you properly.”

sequence._describe: Robin of Loxby and his father walking together back toward the camp fire, an uncertain but softening distance between them, Marian Fletcher leading the way. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, warm late-afternoon lighting, cautiously hopeful mood.

text: Marian, watching the whole exchange with careful attention, finally stepped forward, her voice carrying the particular calm authority she brought to any moment requiring it. “Then let's talk properly,” she said, “somewhere the whole camp can hear what needs hearing, rather than standing here at the treeline like strangers deciding whether to trust each other.”
“That's fair,” the man said, dismounting slowly, careful of Robin's continued wariness. “More than fair, given everything.”

Robin said nothing for a long moment, simply looking at his father — older, worn, carrying himself like a man who'd finally run out of safer alternatives — and found, beneath the tangled mess of anger and confusion and cautious hope, something he hadn't expected to feel at all.

Relief. Not forgiveness, not yet, not something so simple or so quickly arrived at. But relief, plain and real, that whatever had kept them apart all these years was finally, properly, about to be spoken aloud between them.

“Come to the fire, then,” Robin said, finally, the words costing him something to offer but offered all the same. “You've clearly ridden hard to reach me. The least I can do is hear you out properly, whatever it costs either of us to finally say it.”

They walked back into camp together, father and son, an uncertain distance still very much between them, but a distance that had, for the first time in years, actually begun — however cautiously — to close.
